cards.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — The Core Exploit
cards.teaser: XSS is not about crossing sites in the geographic sense — it is about an attacker's JavaScript executing inside a victim's browser session, inheriting full access to that session's cookies, DOM, and network origin.

runs.text: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) occurs when an attacker successfully injects a script payload into a web page that is subsequently rendered and executed by another user's browser. The name is historical and slightly misleading; the essential mechanism is
foreign code gaining same-origin privileges
in a victim's browsing context.

Once an attacker's script runs in the victim's browser session it has access to everything the legitimate JavaScript can access: session cookies (if not HttpOnly), the full DOM, stored credentials in localStorage, and the ability to make authenticated requests to the same origin. The attacker's script is not impersonating the user from outside — it
is
the user, as far as the browser and the server are concerned.

items.text: — steal the session cookie and replay it from the attacker's machine.
— inject a fake login form, capture credentials as the user types.
listener and exfiltrate every keystroke to an attacker-controlled endpoint.

— redirect the browser to a drive-by download page. The Samy worm (MySpace, 2005) exploited stored XSS to self-propagate; it infected over one million profiles in under 20 hours — the fastest-spreading internet worm at the time.

runs.text: XSS has ranked in the OWASP Top 10 every year since its inception. Browser sandbox bypasses, CSP bypasses, and DOM-based variants keep it relevant even as frameworks add default escaping. It is the most common client-side vulnerability class.

XSS means an attacker's script is running inside your user's browser, pretending to be your site. The browser trusts it completely — because it came from your origin — so it can steal cookies, read the DOM, and make requests the user never intended.

cards.title: Reflected XSS — The URL-Borne Payload
cards.teaser: In reflected XSS the attacker's payload travels in the URL, gets echoed into the HTTP response, and executes in the victim's browser — all in a single request/response cycle. The server never stores it; the victim's click is the trigger.

runs.text: Reflected XSS follows a simple three-step pattern:

items.text: Attacker crafts a URL containing a script payload in a query parameter:
Victim clicks the link (via phishing email, forum post, or shortened URL). The browser sends the request to the legitimate server.
The server echoes the unescaped query value into the HTML response. The victim's browser renders the page and executes the injected script in the bank's origin.

runs.text: A classic vulnerable server-side pattern (PHP):

Reflected XSS requires the attacker to trick the victim into clicking a crafted URL. This makes it less severe at scale than stored XSS, but it remains dangerous in targeted attacks. The eBay XSS vulnerabilities discovered in 2014 allowed attackers to inject scripts via product listing URLs; phishing emails directing buyers to crafted URLs could steal eBay session cookies.

Modern browsers shipped the XSS Auditor as a reflected-XSS mitigation, but it was subsequently removed (Chrome 78, 2019; Firefox never shipped it) because it was bypassable, introduced new information-leak vulnerabilities, and created false confidence. CSP is the correct mitigation.
Reflected XSS: the payload is in the URL, the server bounces it back in the response, and it runs in the victim's browser. The server never saves it — the attack lives and dies in one round trip.

cards.title: Stored XSS — The Persistent Payload
cards.teaser: Stored XSS is persisted server-side and delivered to every user who visits the infected page — one injection, unlimited victims. It requires no victim interaction beyond normal site usage.

runs.text: Stored (persistent) XSS occurs when an attacker submits a payload that the server saves — in a database, a log, a comment thread, a user profile — and then later serves to other users without encoding it. Unlike reflected XSS, there is no crafted URL; the attack propagates through normal site usage.

The Samy worm (2005) is the textbook example: Samy Kamkar stored a payload in his MySpace profile that, when any logged-in user viewed the profile, added Samy as a friend, copied the worm to the viewer's own profile, and displayed the message "but most of all, Samy is my hero." Because the payload propagated through profile views — an everyday social action — it replicated exponentially. One million profiles were infected in 20 hours before MySpace was taken offline to contain it.
Common stored XSS injection points:

items.text: File names of uploaded files (if the name is rendered in HTML)

runs.text: Storing sanitized HTML in a database is not the same as storing raw user input — but sanitization libraries have their own bypass histories. The safest approach is to store raw user content and encode it at render time for the specific output context (HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript, URL).

Stored XSS saves the payload to a database. Every user who loads the page executes the attacker's script — no phishing required. One injection, unlimited victims for as long as the payload sits in the database.

cards.title: DOM-Based XSS — The Server-Invisible Attack
cards.teaser: In DOM-based XSS the payload never reaches the server — client-side JavaScript reads attacker-controlled data from the URL or browser APIs and writes it into the DOM unsafely. Server-side output encoding cannot stop it.

runs.text: DOM-based XSS occurs entirely in the browser. The server sends a perfectly safe HTML page; the danger is in what the page's own JavaScript does with data from
sources
(attacker-controlled inputs) and
sinks
(DOM APIs that execute or render content).
Common sources:
Common sinks:
Because the payload is in the URL fragment (the part after
), it is never sent to the server in the HTTP request. Server logs show no trace of the attack.

DOM XSS is a browser-side bug. The server sends safe HTML; the page's own JavaScript reads a tainted value from the URL and writes it into the DOM without encoding. No server log entry, no server-side fix — only the client-side code matters.

cards.title: XSS Defenses — Output Encoding and Contextual Escaping
cards.teaser: The fundamental XSS defense is output encoding: transform every character that has special meaning in the rendering context before inserting user-supplied data. The encoding rules differ by context — HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript, CSS, URL — and mixing them up is a vulnerability.

runs.text: Output encoding works by ensuring that user-supplied data is treated as
data
, never as
markup or code
. The correct encoding depends on where in the page the value appears:

items.text: encode all non-alphanumeric characters as HTML entities. Attributes
use JSON encoding for data values; never embed user input directly in a

runs.text: Modern frameworks apply contextual escaping automatically when you use them correctly:

Framework-default escaping covers the common case. Bypasses — dangerouslySetInnerHTML, bypassSecurityTrustHtml, v-html — disable the protection and require manual review on every usage. A code-review rule that flags these patterns is a low-cost, high-value control.

Encode data before you put it in the page, using the right encoding for that specific spot. HTML context, attribute context, JavaScript context, and URL context each have different dangerous characters. Get the context wrong and encoding fails.

cards.title: Content Security Policy (CSP) — The Modern XSS Mitigation
cards.teaser: CSP is an HTTP response header that tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, and other resources are legitimate. A well-crafted strict CSP can prevent XSS payloads from executing even when the underlying encoding has failed.

runs.text: Content Security Policy is delivered as an HTTP response header (or a
<meta>
tag, though the header is preferred). The browser parses the policy and enforces it: any resource load or inline script that violates the policy is blocked.
A naive allowlist-based CSP is commonly bypassable. The recommended approach is a
nonce-based strict CSP
Each directive explained:

items.text: — a cryptographically random value generated per request. Only inline scripts carrying the matching
attribute execute. Injected scripts cannot know the per-request nonce.
— allows scripts loaded by a nonced script to also execute, enabling dynamic script loading without whitelisting domains (which is trivially bypassed via CDN JSONP endpoints).
— alternative to nonce; the policy lists the SHA-256/384/512 hash of each permitted inline script. Useful for static pages where scripts don't change.
tag injection, which would redirect all relative URLs.

runs.text: CSP violations can be reported to a collection endpoint via the report-to directive, giving visibility into both attack attempts and misconfigured policies. Use Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only during rollout to collect violations before enforcing.

CSP is a header that tells the browser: only run scripts that I explicitly authorized with a nonce. Even if an attacker injects a script tag, the browser blocks it because the injected tag lacks the per-request nonce. It's a second line of defense after encoding.

cards.title: Trusted Types — DOM XSS Prevention via Type Enforcement
cards.teaser: Trusted Types is a browser API that restricts which values can be assigned to dangerous DOM sinks by requiring them to be wrapped in a validated Trusted Type object — preventing DOM XSS at the language level rather than through encoding conventions.

runs.text: DOM-based XSS sinks like
innerHTML
accept any string. Trusted Types changes that: when enabled, the browser requires that values assigned to dangerous sinks are instances of specific Trusted Type classes (
TrustedHTML
TrustedScript
TrustedScriptURL
). Raw strings are rejected.
Trusted Types are enabled via CSP:
In JavaScript, a policy defines a sanitizer that produces Trusted Type objects:
The practical benefit: Trusted Types reduces all DOM XSS sinks to a small set of explicitly defined policy functions. A security review need only audit those policy functions, not every use of
innerHTML
across the codebase. Google reports that migrating large applications to Trusted Types moves the attack surface from thousands of potential sink locations to a handful of policy definitions.

Trusted Types are supported in Chromium-based browsers and Safari (as of 2025). Angular's DomSanitizer integrates with Trusted Types automatically when the API is available. React does not yet use Trusted Types natively, but the dangerouslySetInnerHTML API still benefits because React itself only writes to the DOM at known, auditable points.

Trusted Types makes the browser refuse to accept plain strings in dangerous DOM positions like innerHTML. Only objects produced by an approved policy — which runs a sanitizer — are accepted. Attack surface shrinks from thousands of string assignments to a few policy functions.

cards.title: Subresource Integrity (SRI) — Hash-Pinning External Scripts
cards.teaser: SRI lets you specify the expected cryptographic hash of an external script or stylesheet. If a CDN serves a tampered file, the browser detects the hash mismatch and refuses to execute it — protecting against CDN compromise and supply-chain attacks.

runs.text: When you load a script from a third-party CDN, you implicitly trust that CDN to serve exactly the file you expect. SRI breaks that implicit trust by giving you a verifiable commitment:
How SRI works:

items.text: attribute contains a base64-encoded SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 hash of the expected file content.
When the browser fetches the resource, it hashes the response body and compares it to the expected hash.
If the hashes match, the resource is loaded. If they differ — due to CDN compromise, cache poisoning, or any tampering — the browser blocks it and logs a violation.
is required for cross-origin resources (CORS must be enabled on the CDN).

runs.text: SRI has a key limitation: it only works for
static
resources. It cannot be applied to dynamically-versioned URLs (e.g.,
latest.js
). For first-party resources served from the same origin, SRI adds no value — the network path is already under your control.
Generate SRI hashes with: openssl dgst -sha384 -binary lodash.min.js | openssl base64 -A — or use the srihash.org web tool. The MDN SRI generator is also available for common CDN libraries.

SRI is a hash lock on external files. You declare what the file should look like; the browser checks the downloaded file's fingerprint before executing it. CDN gets hacked and serves a different file? Hash mismatch, script blocked.

cards.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) — Abusing Ambient Authority
cards.teaser: CSRF abuses the fact that browsers automatically attach cookies to every request made to a site — including requests initiated by a different site. An attacker's page can silently make authenticated requests on the victim's behalf.

runs.text: CSRF exploits the browser's cookie model: cookies are attached based on the
destination
of a request, not its
origin
. If a user is logged in to
bank.com
(session cookie present), and visits
evil.com
, a form on evil.com that submits to
bank.com/transfer
will carry the bank session cookie.

explanation.code:
<!-- evil.com — auto-submits on page load -->
<body onload="document.forms[0].submit()">
  <form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">
    <input type="hidden" name="to" value="attacker_account">
    <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="10000">
  </form>
</body>

runs.text: The bank's server receives a POST request with the victim's session cookie. Without CSRF protection, it looks exactly like a legitimate transfer. The bank has no way to distinguish this request from one the user intentionally submitted.
CSRF attacks are limited to what the victim can do — reading response bodies from cross-site requests is blocked by the Same-Origin Policy. CSRF is about
side effects
: state-changing operations (transfers, password resets, account linking) triggered without victim knowledge.

GET requests must never cause state changes — not because of CSRF alone, but because any resource that caches or embeds a URL (an img tag, a link preview) will trigger GET requests. State changes must use POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE.

CSRF tricks your browser into sending a real, cookie-authenticated request to a site you are logged in to — from a page on a completely different site. The server sees a valid cookie and acts on it, unaware the user never intended the request.

cards.title: CSRF Defenses — Tokens, Double-Submit, and Custom Headers
cards.teaser: CSRF defenses work by adding something a cross-site attacker cannot know or forge: a secret token synchronized with the server, a custom request header, or a cookie value that must be echoed in the request body.

runs.text: The classic CSRF defenses, ranked from most to least robust:

items.text: The server generates a cryptographically random per-session (or per-request) token, embeds it as a hidden form field, and validates it on every state-changing request. An attacker cannot read this token from a cross-origin page (blocked by SOP). This is the traditional gold standard.

Set a random value in a cookie and also require that value to be present in a request header or body. A cross-origin attacker cannot read the cookie value (SOP), so cannot echo it. Works well for stateless APIs but is weakened if an attacker can set cookies (e.g., via XSS or subdomain takeover).
AJAX requests can include a custom header (e.g.,
). Cross-origin requests cannot set arbitrary custom headers without CORS preflight — so the server can reject any request missing the header. Simple, but relies on CORS enforcement.
header matches the expected domain. Fragile — some browsers omit the header in certain scenarios, and it is easily bypassed by same-origin attacker code.

runs.text: Modern best practice: combine a
SameSite=Lax
or
SameSite=Strict

session cookie (covered in the next card) with a CSRF token for defense-in-depth. SameSite alone handles most CSRF vectors; a token handles edge cases like browser support gaps and top-level navigation forgery.

CSRF defenses add a secret the attacker cannot read from another origin: a per-request token in a hidden field, a cookie value echoed in the body, or a custom request header. An attacker's page can trigger the request but cannot include the secret, so the server rejects it.

cards.title: SameSite Cookies — Strict, Lax, and the Default Lax Change
cards.teaser: The SameSite cookie attribute controls whether a cookie is sent on cross-site requests. Lax and Strict prevent most CSRF vectors without any application-level token logic. Chrome's 2020 default-to-Lax change silently improved security for millions of sites.

runs.text: SameSite has three values:

items.text: sent on cross-site requests, including top-level navigations. Provides the strongest CSRF protection. Downside: the cookie is not sent when a user follows an external link to your site, so they will not appear logged in until they navigate within your site.

— the cookie is sent on cross-site top-level GET navigations (clicking a link) but not on subresource requests (img, script, iframe) or POST/PUT/DELETE requests from another site. Prevents form-based CSRF while preserving login-persistence when following links.
— the cookie is sent on all cross-site requests. Required for third-party cookies (OAuth flows, embedded widgets, payment iframes).

runs.text: In February 2020, Chrome 80 changed the default: cookies without an explicit SameSite attribute began behaving as
SameSite=Lax
. Sites that relied on cross-site cookie delivery for third-party integrations had to explicitly set
SameSite=None; Secure
. For the majority of sites, this change silently improved CSRF resistance with no code changes required.

explanation.code:
# Session cookie — best practice
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

# Third-party embedded widget cookie
Set-Cookie: widget_pref=dark; Secure; SameSite=None; Path=/

runs.text: SameSite=Lax does not protect against all CSRF: a GET-based state-changing endpoint is still attackable via top-level navigation. This is why GET must never cause side effects. SameSite=Lax + no GET side effects = robust CSRF protection without application tokens.

SameSite=Lax means your session cookie only travels when the user intentionally navigates to your site — not when another site triggers a hidden request behind the scenes. Strict adds even more restriction. None keeps the old unsafe behavior, but requires HTTPS.

cards.title: Clickjacking — UI Redress and Frame Controls
cards.teaser: Clickjacking overlays an invisible iframe of a target site over a decoy page. The victim thinks they are clicking a game button or prize claim; they are actually clicking a bank transfer confirm or an OAuth approval on the target site.

runs.text: Clickjacking (UI redress attack) exploits the browser's ability to embed any page in an iframe. The attacker:

items.text: Creates a page with an attractive UI ("Click here to claim your prize!").
Places an iframe of the target site (e.g.,
, aligned so the confirm button lines up with the prize claim button.
The victim clicks the visible decoy button, which actually clicks the invisible confirm button inside the iframe.

runs.text: Clickjacking defenses:

items.text: prevents the page from being framed at all.
allows framing only by the same origin.
allows only same-origin frames. Supported by all browsers, but less flexible than CSP (cannot allowlist specific origins).

explanation.code:
# Modern approach — CSP frame-ancestors
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';

# Legacy fallback — send both for older browser coverage
X-Frame-Options: DENY

runs.text: frame-ancestors in CSP cannot be set in a <meta> tag — it must be in the HTTP response header. X-Frame-Options can also only be set in a header, not via meta. Both headers must be applied on all pages that contain sensitive actions, not just the home page.

Clickjacking hides your site inside an invisible iframe on the attacker's page, aligned so your sensitive button sits behind their visible button. The fix is to refuse to be framed: frame-ancestors 'none' in CSP, or X-Frame-Options: DENY.

cards.title: CORS — What It Allows and What It Does Not
cards.teaser: CORS is widely misunderstood: it relaxes the Same-Origin Policy for reading responses, but it does not protect against CSRF, and a misconfigured CORS policy can expose data to any origin. The preflight request is the browser's safety check, not the server's.

runs.text: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) prevents JavaScript on
evil.com
from reading responses from
api.bank.com
. CORS is a mechanism by which
api.bank.com
can opt in to sharing responses with specific trusted origins.
The CORS handshake for non-simple requests uses a preflight:

items.text: If approved, the browser sends the actual request.

runs.text: Common CORS misconfigurations:

items.text: effectively grants access to every origin — same as
but potentially worse because it works with
allows sandboxed iframes and some redirect chains — effectively attacker-controlled.
is rejected by browsers — but the attempt to use this pattern signals a misunderstood requirement.

runs.text: CORS does not prevent the request from reaching the server — it prevents the browser from giving the response to the calling script. The server still processes the request. CORS is not a substitute for authentication or CSRF protection.

CORS lets a server say: 'I trust this other origin to read my responses.' The browser enforces it — the request still goes out, but the browser hides the response from the calling page unless the server explicitly allows it. Misconfiguring it to echo any origin back is the same as having no protection at all.

cards.title: The Same-Origin Policy — Exceptions and Cross-Origin Isolation
cards.teaser: The SOP has deliberate exceptions: CORS, postMessage, and the now-deprecated document.domain. Cross-origin isolation (COOP + COEP) goes further, enabling high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer while preventing Spectre-style leaks.

runs.text: The Same-Origin Policy defines "same origin" as the combination of scheme + host + port. It blocks cross-origin
reads
but allows cross-origin
embeds
(iframes, images, scripts). Its deliberate exceptions:

items.text: — a server-declared opt-in that allows specific cross-origin reads. Requires cooperation from the server (previous card).
— allows any two browsing contexts to exchange messages regardless of origin. The receiver must validate
and then access each other's DOM. Chrome deprecated this in 2022 — it broadened the attack surface significantly if any subdomain was compromised.

runs.text: Cross-origin isolation is a stricter mode enabled by two headers:

explanation.code:
# Cross-Origin Opener Policy — isolates the browsing context group
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin

# Cross-Origin Embedder Policy — blocks embeds not opted in to CORS or CORP
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp

runs.text: When both headers are set, the page is cross-origin isolated:
crossOriginIsolated
is true,
SharedArrayBuffer

is available, and high-resolution timers are re-enabled. Crucially, cross-origin isolation prevents other origins from sharing a process with the page, which mitigates Spectre-class side-channel attacks that use precise timers to read cross-process memory.

postMessage security rule: always specify the target origin as the second argument to postMessage(), never '*'. On the receiver, always check event.origin before trusting the message. An unvalidated postMessage receiver is a cross-origin communication channel open to any site.

The SOP has three official escape hatches: CORS for server-approved cross-origin reads, postMessage for explicit cross-origin messaging, and document.domain which is now deprecated for being too dangerous. Cross-origin isolation locks everything down further to prevent Spectre attacks.

cards.title: Putting It Together — A Defense-in-Depth Header Stack
cards.teaser: No single defense eliminates all cross-site attack vectors. A mature application layers encoding, CSP, SameSite cookies, framing controls, and CORS together so that failure of any single control does not equal compromise.

runs.text: A defense-in-depth response header stack for a typical web application:
The defense layers, and what each stops:

items.text: — prevents injection into the HTML page. First line of XSS defense.
— blocks injected script execution even if encoding fails.
— prevents DOM XSS by type-enforcing dangerous sink assignments.
— stops CSRF edge cases not covered by SameSite.
— prevents data exfiltration via cross-origin reads.

runs.text: Use securityheaders.com or the Google CSP Evaluator to grade your headers. A common pitfall: CSP is set on the home page but not on API responses or redirect pages. Every response that could carry sensitive content or trigger script execution needs the full header set.

No single header stops all cross-site attacks. The stack works as a series of independent backstops: encoding stops most XSS, CSP catches what encoding misses, SameSite handles CSRF, frame-ancestors stops clickjacking. Each layer assumes the ones before it might fail.
